_note: Editorial layer on top of data/laws.json (which is imported from the manuscript). Everything here was authored for the site build and needs editorial review: roles, plain-terms summaries, checklist questions, presets and claim-checker rules. Questions marked source=handoff came from the design handoff's content.json; source=derived were rewritten from each law's own 'Use it' section.

goodharts-law.plainTerms: If you reward people or models for hitting a number, they get good at the number. Whether they got better at the actual job is a separate question that needs its own check.
questions: Which metric did you optimize during training and model selection, and is the reported score on that same metric?
Was the reported test set ever used for tuning, prompt iteration, or choosing between checkpoints?
Show us five outputs that score highly but are still wrong. What do they have in common?
What will you measure after launch, and who decides when that metric has stopped being useful?

workedExample.text: A support assistant is tuned to raise CSAT. It learns to close tickets with a cheerful summary before the problem is solved. CSAT goes up; repeat contacts go up too.

campbells-law.plainTerms: The more a score decides who gets funded, hired, or bought, the more people bend their work around the score. The damage reaches the work itself, not just the number.
questions: Does a real decision rest on a single ranking, or on at least two independent measures plus a qualitative review?
How many variants, seeds, or prompts were tried before this result was reported?

the-construct-gap.plainTerms: A test called "reasoning" only measures how a system does on that test's items, in that format. Whether that says anything about reasoning in general needs its own evidence.
questions: Which of our real tasks does this benchmark resemble, and how was that checked?
What would a high score here fail to tell us?

the-functionality-fallacy.plainTerms: Before asking whether an AI system is fair or safe, ask whether it works at all. Plenty of deployed systems fail at their stated job, and a vendor's claim is not evidence.
questions: What evidence shows the system works on data like ours, gathered by someone other than the vendor?
What does the system do when it's wrong, and how often does that happen?

the-metric-mirage.plainTerms: The scoring method is part of the result. Score the same outputs a different way and a sudden leap can turn into steady progress, or the reverse.
questions: Does the result hold when it is re-scored with a second, continuous metric?
Were the metrics chosen, with the reasons written down, before the results were seen?

benchmark-saturation.plainTerms: Tests stop being useful once everyone scores near the top. The remaining differences are mostly noise, and the real gaps are somewhere else.
questions: How close are top systems to this benchmark's ceiling?
Is there a newer or harder test that still separates systems?

data-contamination.plainTerms: If a model saw the test questions while it was training, a high score may only mean it remembers them. Fresh or private questions are the reliable check.
questions: What overlap analysis was run between the test set and the training data?
Were results confirmed on data created after the training cutoff?

adaptive-overfitting.plainTerms: Each time you adjust a prompt or a model because of how it did on the test, the test tells you a little less. Keep a locked test that you use only to decide.
questions: Is there a locked test set, kept separate from the dev set used for iteration?
How many times has the locked test set been consulted to make decisions?

the-clever-hans-effect.plainTerms: A model can pass a test by picking up an accidental pattern, such as a watermark or a telltale word, instead of the skill you meant to test. Build cases where the shortcut fails.
questions: Was a partial-input baseline run to see whether accuracy stays high without the part of the input that should matter?
Do contrast pairs or behavioral tests show the model gets the right answers for the right reasons?

the-gold-standard-myth.plainTerms: The answer key and the human ratings are measurements too, and they contain errors and disagreement. Treat them as evidence, not as ground truth.
questions: How often do independent raters agree on the labels, and was that measured before the labels were trusted?
Who audited the labels on the items where strong models disagree with the answer key?

prompt-sensitivity.plainTerms: Small changes in wording or formatting can swing a model's score. A result from one prompt is a result for that prompt.
questions: How much does the score move across reasonable rephrasings?
Was the prompt tuned on the test set?

judge-bias.plainTerms: Using an AI to grade AI is fast and cheap, but graders have favorites: the first answer, the longer answer, and answers that sound like their own. Check the grader against people.
questions: Was the AI grader checked against human judgments on a sample?
Were answer order and length controlled for, and is the grader from the same model family?

criteria-drift.plainTerms: You work out what "good" means by reading real outputs, so your rubric will change as you grade. Version it, and re-grade a fixed set when it does.
questions: Was the rubric written after reading real outputs, and is it versioned with a date and a reason for each change?
When the criteria changed, was a fixed reference set re-graded so trends stay comparable?

once-is-not-reliable.plainTerms: A system that works once may fail the next time. Customers live with the all-runs-pass rate, not the best-run rate.
questions: How many runs per item, and what is the pass rate across all of them?
Is the result reported as pass@1, pass@k, or passing on every run?

the-cost-frontier.plainTerms: You can buy accuracy with more compute, so a score without its cost is half a result. Compare systems at matched cost, or show the whole tradeoff.
questions: What did each task cost in tokens or dollars, and what was the latency, next to every accuracy number?
Was a cheap baseline, such as a single call, a smaller model, or a simple retry loop, included at a matched budget?

no-error-bars-no-result.plainTerms: Every score is an estimate. If two systems differ by less than the noise, nobody has shown that they differ.
questions: What is the 95% confidence interval on each score, and how many items and runs does it rest on?
Is the gap between systems larger than the interval, using a paired comparison on the same items?

the-averaging-trap.plainTerms: A strong average can hide a group the system fails badly. Report results for the groups that matter, and show the worst one.
questions: Which user groups, languages, or input types matter here, and were results reported for each?
What is the worst-performing slice, and does it have enough examples to support its own error bars?

the-baseline-rule.plainTerms: A win is only as strong as what it beat. Compare against the simplest thing that could work and today's actual process, with the same tuning effort.
questions: Was the current process, or the simplest thing that could work, included as a baseline?
Did the baselines get the same tuning budget as the new method?

the-benchmark-lottery.plainTerms: Which benchmarks get reported can decide who looks best. Pick the suite before you see results, and read the whole table.
questions: Was the benchmark suite chosen and written down before any results were seen?
Which common benchmarks are missing from the results table, and why?

the-reproducibility-rule.plainTerms: If nobody can rerun an evaluation, it is an anecdote. Record the model version, prompts, settings, data, and scoring code, and save the raw outputs.
questions: Are the model version, system prompt, decoding settings, dataset version, and scoring code recorded so the eval can be rerun?
Are raw outputs saved, and is there a canary set to rerun whenever the vendor updates the model?

presence-not-absence.plainTerms: An evaluation can show that a capability or a risk exists. It can't show that none does, only that it wasn't found with this much effort.
questions: How hard did anyone try to elicit this capability or failure: which prompts, tools, fine-tuning, and how many attempts?
Who red-teamed this, and do they have real domain expertise?

evaluation-awareness.plainTerms: Models can often tell a test from real use, and may behave differently under test. Pair pre-launch tests with monitoring of real use.
questions: Are the eval scenarios built from real, messy usage, or do they look obviously synthetic?
How does behavior in the eval compare with behavior in monitored real use?

distribution-shift.plainTerms: A score measured on one group of people, places, or times doesn't automatically carry over to another. Test on data from where the system will actually run.
questions: When was the test data collected, and from which users?
How does it compare with current production inputs?

the-lab-to-field-gap.plainTerms: A system that works in the lab can fail in real conditions: workflows, time pressure, lighting, bandwidth, and people. Watch it in use before calling it validated.
questions: What changed for real users in a pilot, measured how?
Which lab results did not hold up in the pilot?

the-team-is-the-system.plainTerms: When people work with AI, the person and the AI together produce the outcome. Test them together, including how often people accept advice that is wrong.
questions: Was the person plus the AI tested together, and compared with the human alone and the AI alone?
How accurate are people on the cases where the AI is wrong?

the-jagged-frontier.plainTerms: AI can excel at a task that seems hard and fail at one that seems easy, and people can't see where the edge is. Map it for your own tasks with direct tests.
questions: Were tasks that are easy for people tested, not only hard ones?
Where are the known failure pockets, and are users told about them?

categories._note: One-line thread per part, used in the quick brief's overview. Authored for the build; needs editorial review.

I.thread: A score stands in for something you care about, so check what it really measures and what is pushing on it.

II.thread: The test can be stale, leaked, tuned against, or wrong, so decide how far to trust it before you trust the score.

III.thread: How you run an evaluation changes the number: prompts, graders, criteria, repeat runs, and cost all matter.

IV.thread: How you read the numbers changes the conclusion: noise, averages, baselines, selection, and whether anyone can rerun it.

V.thread: A benchmark cannot show what happens when real people use the system in real conditions.

laws.why: The score is on a public benchmark. Check whether the test items overlap with the training data.
A headline number is reported without an interval or a count of items and runs.
A benchmark measures what its items test, not what its name says.
Near the ceiling of a benchmark, small gaps carry little information.
If anyone iterated against this benchmark, it is a target rather than a measure.
A comparison is only as strong as the baseline it beats.
A win is claimed with no interval or number of runs.
Which benchmarks are reported can decide who wins.
Systems that cost very different amounts to run are not a fair comparison.
An average gap can hide the groups where the system loses.
Competitor numbers are only comparable if they came from the same prompts, settings, and scoring code.
Rankings that drive buying and press attention invite gaming, including selective reporting of variants.
Optimizing for votes can raise the number without raising quality.
A win rate averages over who voted and what they asked.
Human ratings are measurements with error, and raters disagree.
A win rate is an estimate and needs an interval.
Check which comparisons were left out.
An AI grader has known biases: answer order, answer length, and a preference for its own writing.
A grader is only as good as the human labels it was checked against.
AI-graded scores are still estimates and need intervals.
Rubrics change as people read real outputs. Check whether the criteria were versioned.
The grader's own prompt affects the scores it gives.

types.label: Production accuracy
types.detect: \b(in production|production|real[- ]world|real users?|customers?|deployed|in the field|live traffic|pilot|in practice)\b

laws.why: Vendor-reported performance is a claim. Independent validation on your own population is evidence.
Performance on one population does not automatically carry over to another.
Real use adds workflows, time pressure, and people that the lab left out.
Production accuracy is an average. Check the worst-performing groups.
Customer-facing results depend on how often it works every time, not once.
Behavior under test may differ from behavior in real use, so check monitoring.

modifiers.why: An internal benchmark that the team also iterated on is a target, not a measure.
A test the team built and reuses is easy to tune against without noticing.
"Superhuman" on a benchmark often signals saturation, contamination, or both.
"Superhuman" on a benchmark often signals saturation, contamination, or both.
A failed attempt to find a risk says how hard someone tried, not whether the risk exists.
Explanations can raise trust without raising accuracy.
A demo is not evidence from real use.
Perfect-sounding claims need evidence from repeated runs.
A model grading its own outputs tends to favor them.
An average cannot show who the system fails.
Accuracy without cost is half a result.

situationFinder._note: Situation finder rules. Each situation maps a described circumstance to the laws a careful reader would check first, in the same shape as the claim-checker types. Authored for the site build and needs editorial review.
situationFinder.example: We are about to launch an AI assistant that helps recruiters screen resumes. We tested it on our own benchmark and had another model grade the answers, but nobody has checked how it does for different groups of applicants.

laws.why: You are deciding whether to rely on a system you did not build. Before comparing options, ask for evidence that any of them works on data like yours.
Vendors usually show scores on tests with impressive names. Check that those tests resemble the work you need done.
A vendor's win only counts against a fair comparison. Ask what it beat, and whether your current process was in the comparison.
Which benchmarks appear in a vendor's table can decide who looks best. Ask which common ones are missing.
Public benchmark scores may reflect memorized test items. Ask how overlap with training data was ruled out.
Two options can score the same at very different cost. Ask for cost and latency next to every accuracy number.
A vendor's result you cannot rerun is an anecdote. Check that the setup is recorded well enough for you to repeat it.

situations.label: Building our own evaluation
situations.detect: \b((build|building|design|designing|create|creating|set up|setting up|start(ing)?|write|writing|develop(ing)?)\b[^.]{0,25}\b(evals?|evaluations?|test sets?|benchmarks?|golden sets?|rubrics?|eval suite)|no evals?|don'?t have (any )?(evals?|tests?)|how (do|should) we (test|evaluate|measure))\b

laws.why: Your own test set stops being a fair test once you iterate against it. Lock a portion away before you start tuning.
The answer key you build is a measurement with errors. Check how often independent raters agree before you trust it.
A small eval set gives a wide range of plausible scores. Decide how many items and runs you need before comparing anything.
You will learn what good means by reading real outputs, so your rubric will change. Version it and keep a fixed reference set.
Your results will depend on the prompt you choose. Test rephrasings before treating a score as a property of the model.
Pick and justify your metrics before you see results, so the scoring method does not decide the conclusion.
Record the model version, prompts, settings and data from the start, so the eval can be rerun later.
Testing before launch happens in conditions that are cleaner than real use. Plan a pilot and measure what changes for real users.
Your test data comes from a past population. Check how it compares with the inputs you will actually receive.
A good overall score can hide a group the system fails. Decide which user groups matter and report each.
Users meet the all-runs pass rate, not your best run. Measure how often it works every time.
Models can behave differently when they can tell they are being tested. Build launch tests from messy, real usage.
A clean pre-launch test shows you did not find a problem, not that none exists. Ask how hard anyone tried.
Capability is uneven. Test tasks that seem easy to people, not only the hard ones, and tell users where the known gaps are.
Real inputs change over time. Compare current production inputs with the data you tested on.
What users report may not show up in your earlier tests. Find which lab results did not hold in real use.
Once a metric guides decisions it stops being a good measure. Decide who judges when your live metric has stopped being useful.
Compare behavior in your tests with behavior in monitored real use, because the two can differ.
An average over all users can hide the group that is complaining. Look at the worst-performing slice.

situations.label: Using an AI to grade outputs

laws.why: AI graders have favorites, such as longer answers or their own model family. Check the grader against human judgments on a sample.
The grading prompt is your rubric, and it will change as you read outputs. Version it and re-grade a fixed reference set.
Human ratings used to check the grader also contain errors and disagreement. Measure how often raters agree.
The grader is a prompt too. Small changes in how it is asked to score can move results.
If results change between runs, one run is not a result. Report the pass rate across repeated runs.
Differences smaller than the noise are not differences. Put an interval on each score and compare on the same items.
Small changes in wording or formatting can swing a score. Measure how much it moves across reasonable rephrasings.
If you cannot reproduce a result, record the model version, settings and data so you can find out why.
When a system affects people, whether it works comes before whether it is fair. Ask what it does when it is wrong, and how often.
A strong average can hide a group the system fails badly. Report results for the groups that matter.
If a person reviews the output, test the person and the AI together, not the AI alone.
An evaluation cannot prove a harm is absent. Ask who tried to find it and whether they had domain expertise.
In high-stakes areas the labels are often contested. Ask who audited the items where strong models disagree with the answer key.
The person and the AI together produce the outcome. Compare the pair with the human alone and the AI alone.
People cannot see where the AI's edges are. Tell users the known failure pockets, and check which tasks they over-trust it on.
Real workflows add time pressure and interruptions. Measure what changes when people use it for real.

situations.label: Relying on public benchmarks or leaderboards

laws.why: A benchmark measures what it measures, not what its name says. Check how it resembles your real tasks.
Tests stop separating systems once everyone scores near the top. Check how close the leaders are to the ceiling.
Public test items can end up in training data. Ask how overlap was checked and whether newer data confirms the result.
Which benchmarks are shown can decide who wins. Ask which common ones are missing from the table.
Systems get tuned toward well-known benchmarks. Check whether the reported metric was also the one optimized.
An overall score can hide the language or group that fails. Name the groups that matter and report each with its own error bars.
Results on one population do not automatically carry over to another. Check how your test data compares with each group you serve.
Capability is uneven across tasks and groups. Document the known failure pockets and tell users.

situations.label: The team is chasing a number

laws.why: When a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure. Check whether the metric you report is the one you optimized.
The more a number drives decisions, the more people bend their work around it. Back important decisions with independent measures.
Repeated tuning against the same test set makes it worth less each time. Keep a locked set you rarely consult.
The scoring method is part of the result. Check that the gain holds under a second metric.
You can buy accuracy with more compute. Report cost and latency next to every accuracy number and compare at matched cost.
Multi-step systems compound small failure rates. Measure the pass rate across repeated runs of the whole task.
A complex system should beat a simple one tuned just as hard. Give simple baselines the same tuning budget.

situations.label: Safety, red-teaming or 'it never does X'

laws.why: A test can show a risk exists but not that none does. Ask how hard anyone tried and with which tools.
A model that can tell it is being tested may behave differently in real use. Compare test behavior with monitored real behavior.
Whether a jailbreak works can depend on small wording changes. A single attempt is not coverage.
Labels and human ratings are measurements with error. Measure how often independent raters agree before trusting the answer key.
A model can match the labels for the wrong reason. Run partial-input baselines to check it uses the part of the input that should matter.
If the rating guidelines changed, re-grade a fixed reference set so trends stay comparable.

situations.label: Suspiciously good results
situations.detect: \b(shortcuts?|spurious|artifacts?|too good to be true|suspicious(ly)? (high|good)|surprisingly (high|good)|near[- ]perfect|memori[sz](e|ed|ing|ation)|leak(s|ed|age)?|right answer for the wrong)\b

laws.why: A model can get the right answer for the wrong reason. Check whether accuracy holds when the part that should matter is removed.
If the test was in the training data, the score measures memory. Ask what overlap analysis was run and confirm on newer data.
Repeated tuning against the same test makes it flatter you. Check for a locked test set that was rarely used.
